description_full: AppLovin Corporation provides end-to-end artificial intelligence-powered advertising solutions for businesses in the United States and internationally. It operates through two segments, Advertising and Apps. The company offers Axon Ads Manager, a suite of marketing solutions that enables developers to automate, optimize, and manage marketing efforts; MAX, an in-app bidding technology that optimizes the value of a publisher's advertising inventory by running a real-time competitive auction; Adjust, a measurement and analytics marketing platform; and Wurl, a connected TV platform, which distributes streaming video for content companies, provides advertising and publishing solutions. It serves individuals, small and independent businesses, enterprises, advertisers and advertising networks, mobile app publishers, and indie studio developers. The company was incorporated in 2011 and is headquartered in Palo Alto, California.

financial_summary: Applovin Corporation is a large-cap communication services business with a $129.6B market cap on $5.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +25% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.
Accruals are elevated at -8.8% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 20× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.7%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 4.9% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 3.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 76% operating margin runs 67pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.69x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.8% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+100.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 169 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 55% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 47% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 80% and a beta of 1.50, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.05 vs 5y 2.48), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.2B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 90% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 79%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 26.3 vs 14.9 and EV/EBITDA 19.6 vs 9.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an EBIT/EV of 3.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 31 covering analysts target $448 on average, 15% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 12.0%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.30).
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.19x, but high accruals (-8.8% of assets).
ROE of 156% is amplified by 3.4x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 48pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 4.1% of revenue on R&D and 3.8% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.2x net debt to EBITDA ($2.5B of cash against $3.5B of debt), with interest covered 20.1x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 24.8% over 3 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
At current returns, reinvesting 7% of profits supports about 1.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Capex runs only 0.0x depreciation (0.1% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.9%, and institutions hold 77%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (46 sales, net $95.4M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.7% (1.7% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 2.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 876 employees, each generates about $6.3M of revenue, 10.3x the Communication Services median, and productivity has risen 18.4% a year.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $410K (0x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
